title: The forgotten strength
hookLine: cursed to forget his powers until a friend reminds him; who you are can be forgotten, not lost

cards: A child with the strength of the wind, and no sense of limits, runs wild through the forest hermitages. Young Hanuman knocks over the sages' water pots and ritual vessels. He tears their bark clothes.
Not cruel; just a kid who doesn't know his own size. The sages, patient people, reach the end of their patience. They don't take his strength away.
They do something stranger. They curse him to forget it: all that power, and no memory of it, until someone reminds him.

teach.b: Years pass. Hanuman grows up gentle, wise and loyal, with no idea what he can do.
Now jump ahead. Monkeys and bears stand on the shore, staring at the ocean. Somewhere across it is the island of Lanka, a hundred yojanas away, the text says: an enormous distance.
One by one the heroes say how far they could jump. Ten. Twenty.
Fifty. Jambavan, the old bear, says ninety, now that he's old. Prince Angada could make the hundred, but isn't sure he could make it back.
Hanuman sits apart, quiet. He doesn't even volunteer.
Then Jambavan walks over and tells Hanuman his own story. You are the son of the wind. As a baby you leapt for the sun.
Every god gave you a gift. Why are you sitting here silent? As he speaks, Hanuman remembers, and he begins to grow, until the others cheer.
So the strength was never gone. It was forgotten. Some Hindu teachers read this as a picture of the atman, your tenth word: the true self.
In that reading, who you really are can be covered over and forgotten, but never lost, and a teacher's work is to remind you. Jambavan gives no new power. He tells the old story back.
Hindus still do this. The Hanuman Chalisa, forty short verses sung in many homes, tells Hanuman's own deeds: the sun, the ocean, the mountain.
People sing it when they're afraid, calling on the strength those deeds tell of.

how: Many Hindus recite the Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn traditionally credited to the poet Tulsidas, for courage in hard times; it retells Hanuman's deeds, including the crossing of the ocean.

o: the sage who cursed Hanuman to forget his own power
the old bear who reminds Hanuman of the strength he forgot
the monkey prince who could jump but not jump back

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: curse him to forget his power
the old bear who reminds him

s: the sages take Hanuman's strength away
they make him forget it. the strength stays, until someone reminds him.
at the shore, Hanuman volunteers first
he sits apart, quiet, until Jambavan tells him his own story.
the one who lifts the curse is a friend, not a god
the old bear Jambavan reminds him who he is.

games.q: you're Jambavan. everyone has said how far they can jump, and no one can cross. Hanuman sits apart, silent. what do you do?
o: tell the army to turn back.
go and tell Hanuman his own story.
games.why: he reminds Hanuman: son of the wind, the leap for the sun, every god's gift. Hanuman remembers, and grows.

practice: Sit, breathe, and be your own Jambavan for a minute. If you know the Hanuman Chalisa, or another prayer, say a few lines slowly. If you don't, recall a hard thing you got through, or a time you were braver than you expected.
Tell yourself plainly, the way the old bear did: that was you. It still is.

wordCard.voice: Jambavan. The old bear at the ocean's edge who reminds Hanuman of the strength he forgot.

carryVoice: Your line: atman: forgotten, never lost. The true self waits to be remembered. Tomorrow, a meeting in disguise. Day thirty, done.
